review:
Homefront is an FPS which tells the story of a resistance movement fighting back against a near future Korean occupation of the USA.

The game play is a very generic FPS. Pretty much identical to Call of Duty and Medal of Honor; you can only carry two weapons,  and four grenades. You will have to swap to different weapons from dead enemies throughout each level as finding ammo is more difficult than you would imagine. None of the enemies use the same weapon...

Graphics wise, it looks nice, but you can tell the game was released in 2011, it looks better than most games released, however it shows it's age when comparing it to more recent titles. The graphical options are wide and you can probably play this game on a potato if you really wanted.

All the maps in the single player are very well designed, sadly you can't really explore because you are constantly reminded to keep following your squad leader. You fight through various different environments such as the streets of suburbs, department stores, and baseball fields, all of which show a disturbing outcome of the quite scary "what if?" scenario from a Korean invasion.

The single player of Homefront will take about five hours to complete; this is pretty short in my opinion, and the game ends on a massive cliff hanger, I would of liked to have seen another two or three more missions to tire up the loose ends in the story.  Multiplayer is still very much alive in Homefront, I have only played in a couple of games but I had no problem finding a map full of people to jump into. A lot of the reviews you will read on here will say multiplayer is the strongest aspect of the game, so they can't all be wrong. 

I would like to recommend Homefront; however I would wait till it is on sale, it has recently been on sale a few weeks ago for as low as £3,75, which would be an absolute bargain if you could get it for that again in an up coming sale.

I must say that I actually enjoyed this game. However, I cant simply recommend it. The campaign is PAINFULLY short. My first playthrough on the default difficulty only took 3 hours and I was in no rush. This is inexcusable. If you find it for $5 or less, pick it up. Other than that don't bother. I must say that the game was good enough to make me very curious about what Crytek will end up doing with the sequel.

STORY
The story, at least at the beginning, is promising and just about close enough to current affairs to have you interested. However, the game is far too forceful with the "oo look how terrible war is" feeling, which seems to be self-defeating: instead of being subtly led into any sort of realisation/agreement, you just feel like you're constantly being struck by a moral hammer that ends up being incredibly annoying but otherwise ineffective.

The characters are also less than compelling. Perhaps having more time in the story might help (see note below on playtime).

GAMEPLAY
The gameplay itself is ok but I remember the odd restrictions in movement popping up (having to take a specific path rather than being able to jump over certain things was limiting for the gamer who decides to mash every button to get round an obstacle!). 

For some reason, the game dynamics/enemies/tools etc. felt a bit like those in Dishonored (which isn't a bad thing): weird and also quite enjoyable.

GRAPHICS
Not bad at all, can't complain.

PLAYTIME
I think I spent about 4 hours completing this game on the hardest setting and I'm not a super skilled gamer. A first person shooter should take at least twice this time to complete!

SUMMARY
Good gameplay and concept, lacking in story and playtime. Probably only buy if you're bored and the price looks favourable...

I’d heard about Homefront for ages, and its world was always super intriguing, but I never got around to playing it… until recently. Seeing Modern Warfare 4 announce a North Korea-themed plot suddenly reminded me of this ancient classic, and I thought, “Yeah, I need to finally check this out.”

Even though it came out in 2011, the story is set in 2027, with North Korea fully invading the US. Looking back now, it gives a weird kind of time-travel vibe. Most FPS games loves to let you play as a badass American super-soldier, but in Homefront, you’re just a regular resistance fighter. And you’re not storming some desert nuke silo or a secret base in Siberia—you’re fighting on streets, in schools, stadiums, neighborhoods… basically your everyday surroundings. It really tries to make you feel, “What if war broke out in your own backyard?” That perspective is refreshing and clever.

The intro cutscenes and first chapter do a fantastic job of setting up this huge, wild world. You see buses transporting civilians, street executions, occupying troops patrolling, news broadcasts… it immediately makes you ask questions: How did North Korea rise to power? Didn’t the US military fight back? How does this resistance even operate? But sadly, the game never really expands on any of that, leaving the story feeling kind of incomplete—like it starts with a bang but fizzles out.

The world-building aside, the story and character development are… well, weak. Connor, Boone, Rianna, Hopper—your squadmates all have names, but after finishing the game, you can barely tell them apart. And the protagonist? Forget it. In five hours of campaign, the main character has no real motivation, no personality, no growth. Connor goes where he’s told, shoots when he’s told, retreats when he’s told. Even the villain, who looks like a North Korean version of General Shepherd, is poorly handled—he shows up maybe two or three times early on and then disappears. The pacing doesn’t help either: deaths, defeats, counterattacks all happen so fast you barely remember anything.

Combat and level design are nothing special either. Yeah, people might say, “It’s a 2011 game.” But 2011 was golden era for FPS—games like Modern Warfare 3, Battlefield 3, Crysis 2, and Resistance 3 were all out there. By comparison, Homefront just doesn’t stand out, so you can’t excuse it just because it’s old.

The biggest disappointment? This IP never got the love it deserved. I don’t hate the game—I actually really like the concept—but the more I think about it, the more I feel like it could have been amazing. With a bigger budget, better writers, and a proper development team, Homefront could’ve been a legendary FPS. Instead, what we got is… a barely-passable half-finished game.

[h3]7/10[/h3]

First playthrough review time.

Homefront has an interesting story and gives that classic military shooter atmosphere from older FPS games. The campaign is short, but the pacing stays good and the later missions become better than the early parts. The shooting sections are simple and keep the game active from start to finish.

The gameplay is decent overall, though the controls may take a little time to get used to, especially for players more familiar with modern FPS movement. The game also shows its age in some technical areas, but it still works fine for a short campaign experience. 

I actually had this game back around 2012, I think, but after installing it on my Windows XP system it never worked properly. I still do not know the exact reason, but maybe I did not install VC++ or DirectX at that time, or maybe the installation files had some issue.

Overall, Homefront is a solid short FPS game with a good story style and good action. It is a good choice for players who like classic military shooters and want something short and straightforward.

Homefront is an FPS released in 2011, developed by Kaos Studios. It’s basically a Call of Duty-like with a North Korean twist.

Since the 2010s, North Korea has been arming itself to the teeth and gradually invading the world. Two years after the start of the occupation of the United States by this dictatorial regime, the dictatorship is total. Extreme violence reigns, with summary executions in the middle of the street, populations rounded up in makeshift camps or sent to forced labor, and omnipresent propaganda that constantly reminds you that you’re no longer really at home. The atmosphere is heavy and oppressive, creating a real sense of urban guerrilla warfare in occupied territory.

We play as Jacobs, a former US Army pilot just freed from a prisoner bus by a small group of resistance fighters against the communist regime. The team is well put together: Connor, the tough-as-nails leader who’s rough around the edges and strongly reminds you of the good old Reznov from Black Ops; Rianna, the badass teammate who never backs down; and Hopper, the Korean ally, mechanic and super chatty guy who brings a welcome touch of humor. The dialogues and interactions perfectly enhance the immersion in this resistance atmosphere.

The gameplay doesn’t mess around and goes all-in on spectacle. We gun down North Korean soldiers left and right, take out armored vehicles, switch from sniping to vehicle-mounted machine-gunning, and even pilot a combat helicopter. The action is completely frantic: everything is exploding everywhere, planes streak across the battlefield at full speed, and the North Koreans scream like madmen during the fights. The combat and destruction sequences are heavily scripted, but at the time they remain exhilarating and perfectly executed.

The enemies are not very varied but are still threatening. We face heavily equipped North Korean infantry, armored vehicles, helicopters, and even crazy survivalists armed to the teeth who complicate matters and add a layer of unpredictable chaos.

The weapons are varied and satisfying to use: pistol, Kriss Vector, several types of assault rifles (M16, SCAR, ACR, Galil, etc.), M249, sniper rifle, and rocket launchers. We also frequently get to take control of the Goliath, a heavily armed six-wheeled all-terrain armored vehicle that obliterates everything we mark. We quickly tend to abuse it as much as we can, since the "Norks" are so numerous.

Graphically, the game holds up well for 2011 and sits in the same league as FEAR 3, COD Black Ops or Bad Company 2. The urban guerrilla settings in typical American suburbs, with their narrow alleys, parking lots, devastated stores and bridges, are immersive and reinforce that thrilling feeling of fighting hard in the heart of a country that is no longer your own.

There are quite a few minor flaws to point out. The character is a bit too slow, which becomes a handicap when you need to take cover quickly or when an objective is timed. You really feel like you’re controlling a big asthmatic lump, and I know what I’m talking about. The weapons have very limited ammo reserves, which forces us to switch them frequently. Object hitboxes are sometimes too large, shooting an enemy hiding behind a thin or wooden surface doesn’t always kill him, and some scripts are questionable, to say the least. Clipping and aliasing are noticeable, and the object draw distance is ridiculously low. To top it all off, the campaign is quite short, five to six hours maximum, which leaves a slightly bitter aftertaste.

Despite all these technical flaws and the very linear and scripted feel, Homefront remains a decent and likeable FPS. Let’s just say it’s a solid B-tier Call of Duty that will give you a few hours of fun, nothing more.

I honestly had a really good time with Homefront. I know the game got a lot of criticism when it came out, and I can definitely see where some of it comes from, but I still think there’s a good game here. I really enjoyed the setting and the whole idea of fighting through an occupied America. The gameplay feels a bit dated now, and there are definitely some rough edges, but it never stopped me from having fun. It’s far from perfect, but I genuinely think Homefront is a solid and underrated game that’s worth experiencing.

Right now, this Homefront is right where it belongs. Mixed reviews, the price that fell from usual 60$ (still, sales up to 90% recommended)... And yet, it's not all that bad.

As a straight-forward shooter with a rather short single-player campaign and not-so-bright multiplayer, it's not worth much. I don't like the Call of Duty series, but this game generally worse at gameplay than Infinity Ward games, and somewhere on the level of Treyarch jobbing. Don't believe those who're saying that there are only 3 hours of gameplay. That comes from people who are playing at easy difficulty. Yeah, the AI is not the brightest bulb in garland, yet the overall challenge is quite fair, weaponry is nice and the overall impression from shootouts is decent enough - if we're not going into ballistics and bullet piercing effects.

The controls are generally good (except for vehicles). The visuals are not bad, on the level with CoD, again. Nothing too fancy, though. The overall viewing angle a bit too small, like we wear an assault helmet - but it is not so! Levels aren't really large, and even when they are - the path is usually quite narrow. Bugs... exists, but not overwhelming. I remember only one rage-producing moment, when I dropped hostile glow hawk, and then trigger moving at the place where I was rammed by some Bradley or whatever, and sending me to restart point. That's bad, yeah, but not really game-breaking. The engine is quite stable, with no crashes, no big troubles that can't be fixed with reloading.

The multiplayer part is not dead - servers (mostly) working, some people are running around and killing each other... usual stuff. I liked the idea that the more kills you perform, the more clear to opposite team your exact position. That's making cheaters more noticeable to others - however, they're still troubled to fair play, admins aren't really any good at the moment. Overall - multiplayer there is a dull and down-sized version of Battlefield 3, so - no, not recommended for MP, without your own team especially.

What I really like about the Homefront - is the amount of backstage work. Of course, it's all quite naive and, as always, made by people who are very far from real warfare business... But still, they're showing quite a nasty and somewhat realistic picture of the former "United States of America", being rounded up and bent by hunger, lack of fuel, the inhumanity of the former citizens, and much more brutality on the part of the mighty Korean warriors. Basically, the story tells that just right after the USA dropped the flag of the world's №1 oppressor, due to financial problems, they got it all back. Right from the 18th century ("The only good American is a dead American"), and particularly, for the US oppressive war of 1950-1953. Yeah, united Koreans, managed to best the US, using their own tactics and arsenal. It supposed to be ironic, but in fact, turns out way too pathetic. The aftertaste of this story is even worse than in the case of Spec Ops the Line... not so strong and bitter, however. That's just a visualized horror of "oh, God, what if the world will do to the US the same thing we're doing to them now? Like in Iraq, Afgan, Libya, etc..." Well, I am more believe in a scenario like in the "Invasion day" 2013 movie - when Americans themselves selling all and everything out.

And still - there is a somewhat good scenario and background work. Videogames are really objects of art, and as one of them, Homefront deserves your brief look. Standard-issue FPS with good guns and story of bent US, spitting in the face of invaders... It worth 6 points from me (out of the usual 10).

To start, I'll recommend VERY cautiously and here's why. It very much feels emotionally detached, like it’s a knock-off Call of Duty 4 that tries to hit its highs in terms of excitement but doesn’t end up doing so for the most part. That being said hypocritically enough, I feel like the game’s best aspects come out in the form of the actual background lore and the evocative imagery, to which I’m also going to fit the atmosphere section alongside the graphics here. 

When the player [spoiler]first gets kidnapped by the “Norks” as Connor would call them, you’re shuttled onto a bus where you witness civilians get lined up to be sent to concentration camps or executed and you’d be forgiven if you thought that it would lead to a bigger payoff. The first level was a decent enough start with a sort of prison break vibe, fighting through hordes of North Koreans as civilians around you become casualties to your rebellion. Then there’s nothing. Then they have a moment in the second mission where you have to jump into a pile of dead bodies to drive home the brutality. Then you have nothing. The third level has you deal with the after effects of dropping White Phosphorus on North Korean soldiers before accidentally hitting yourself with it. Then nothing.[/spoiler] After you get through most of the levels, the game relies on a [spoiler]helicopter mission gimmick (the best level in the entire game by the way)[/spoiler] alongside a finale at the [spoiler]Golden Gate Bridge[/spoiler], which is itself a generous concept that didn’t always deliver for me. The whole background lore of using real life political events involving North Korea before spinning off into its own coalition of several countries actually felt pretty decent and this is where the game shines in a lot of ways. It feels like with Homefront’s ever encompassing scope that the game should’ve followed with its concept of “In-Media-Res”, or hopping in through multiple different perspectives throughout the United States. A bit of Montrose resistance, a bit of U.S. Military camps here and there, maybe someone who was sent to one of these camps to truly drive the nail in. The game feels like it had a lot to work with but kind of stumbled over the pieces right in front of them trying to find some sort of direction. Truth is that I don’t really even know what it says about the politics of a North Korean invasion, other than the obvious of it being bad because they’re a totalitarian regime. This I could fault myself because I’m not always the most literate in fleshing out my explanations per se, but this definitely felt like the writers could’ve gone a bit more in depth with it as well. The atmosphere for the game could be described as brutal for sure in a couple of spots here and there, but otherwise I could’ve considered that average.

In fact, let’s just mix the gameplay sections along with the graphical stuff into the same lack of structure as well, because I feel like this sort of feeling bleeds over into the gameplay aspects. To start out with and to finish the graphical stuff, I feel like the game looks fine enough for the most part despite some obvious budget issues regarding certain things. It seems they’d spend a lot of time grabbing up product placement crossovers like Hooters but at the same time they would fail to provide a personality to the Hooters to make it look like a real restaurant, or at least the remains of a few tables and an empty room or two in the back. They literally have a product placement with the weapons company “Primary Weapons Systems” with their “PWS Diablo SMG” though I couldn’t tell you if it was an actual real SMG (or if any gun wasn’t just a knock-off of real world guns) that in-game isn’t my favorite in the slightest. I remember typing in my notes that “the rest of the guns were okay” but other than that I don’t really remember any sort of standout in terms of which one felt good or even sound good so let’s get that sound design noise off the checklist too. The gameplay itself for the most part feels fine, with your usual shooting of weapons, looting them off corpses, throwing grenades and the expected Call of Duty-isms that you would get from this game (like picking up intel, which while well written looks so cheap and thrown together that it’s kind of sad), enough so I don’t need to explain it. But it feels very rushed, very okay for the most part without a lot of oomph that a lot of older and current first person shooters at the time would deliver on. The helicopter mission was the biggest highlight just because it was both something different with on the ground combat but also because it legitimately felt great with its fluidity and how you could navigate using it. Moving into positives surrounding decent aspects of the game, I would say that whilst I spoke negatively about it in a bunch of ways, if you look past it as average to the point of indifference, I’ll say that it still functions and feels fine enough to where you won’t hate it or get mad at it. Another positive is that despite animations feeling a bit sluggish compared to the well polished feeling of Call of Duty, they’re not terrible and getting a decent resolution with 1920 X 1080 resolution is as easy as typing in “-w 1920 -h 1080” into the Launch Options (no quotations). 

Playing through Homefront was an experience that ended up being kind of exactly how I thought it was gonna be: kind of boring, TEMU Call of Duty on a budget but with interesting ideas that should’ve panned out way more. I didn’t really understand how deep that expectation went with me. Not only did it meet that expectation but it exceeded it. The plot was filled interesting background lore that actually takes into event real world events and a lot of political foreshadowing that felt honestly kind of scary, but aside from certain set pieces and a willingness to show some brutality, it felt like a kind of flat game with flat characters and a flat storyline I wish had more to it. The gameplay felt like the original Modern Warfare, but worse off despite many years ahead of that game. The general atmosphere could be effectively crushing at times but mixed in with some of the shallow characterization and plot development felt like it could be undercooked, and the music for the most part I don’t even remember. As for the voice acting? The actors and actresses do fine, but don’t have the material to really work with here. Some may ask me, why play this? Why not play Call of Duty instead? Sheer curiosity. That’s it. If you’re looking for a game to play through and don’t mind a budgeted look, a cheap game that’ll get you through an afternoon and that’s about it? It’s a fine game to do so, especially because on sale it goes so cheap, but there are also better games to play out there. If you’re curious to try out first person shooters in the vein of OG Call of Duty, it may provide somewhat of a fix but you’ll be left lacking and wishing for more. Like that old phrase goes “it has more bark then bite”. Perhaps its sequel/reboot, Homefront: The Revolution will provide the AA Far Cry fix I sometimes aim for (and surprisingly did pretty well with in terms of Sniper Ghost Warrior: Contracts). Now that I brought that up, perhaps that’s what I’ll need to talk about next.

I brought this way back when the game came out and never really played it due to the polarizing reviews and here's what  I think about it;

Pros -
- Well optimised.
- Fun campaign (just turn your brain off & ignore the cringe that is the loading screens in the game, will talk about it further).
- Fluid gameplay.
- Ruthless AI on harder difficulties.
- The fact that the game predicted 60% of the future events accurately.
- Multiplayer still works and is active.
- Easy achievements.

Cons -
- Short campaign.
- Cringy loading screen quotes, they expect us to give a shit about a "random school teacher" but really I dont, I just want to shoot some NORKS.
- Small MP maps.
- Shitty sound quality.
- Lens flares make you blind af.

Overall it's a fun game and you should give it a try if you're into FPS games, not worth the full price imo.

Did I like this game? Yes, it was reasonably enjoyable.

Do I recommend this game? Currently, no. If I bought, played and wrote a review on this game years ago, I likely would of recommended it.

The Single Player campaign is short, I mean incredibly short. Easily done in 3 hours for your first time.

The Multiplayer ... well ... while it is available, it might as well be non-existant. There are very few players left and apparently if you play "too good" you are likely to be banned from the limited servers available.

The Story is interesting but after the first scene you will probably say to yourself "this sounds familiar". Red Dawn (1984 movie and a 2012 remake) and Tomorrow When The War Begun (2010 movie and 1993-1999 book series), seemed to have a heavy influence on the game.

Graphics are what you expect of a 2010/2011 video game.

Two things also worth mentioning:
1 - This is the first game I have come across that linked with my Logitech G15 keyboard and displayed in game stats (weapon, ammo, mission, etc) on the keyboard's display.
2- The "sequel", Homefront: The Revolution, is more a reboot. Certain aspects of the story (events leading up to the game) differ to this game.

I'm largely recommending this based on nostalgia - I played a shit ton of Homefront multiplayer back in my 360 days. The campaign is nothing special really - honestly, I think the best thing about Homefront was ALWAYS the multiplayer and the campaign is just setting you up for that with a bit of backstory.

The campaign has got some variety like stealth sniping, vehicular combat (e.g. controlling a helicopter and protecting a convoy) - pretty much like Call of Duty in a lot of ways. The friendly AI is annoying and won't shut up but besides that it's just overall pretty generic and it's definitely not going to blow you away. 

The question is; is it worth more than a cup of coffee (since it's on sale)? I'd say yeah. If you can get it while it's 90% off then I think it's definitely worth it. At full price? Absolutely not.  

The campaign is only 3-4 hours long. 

As I said, the game was always about the multiplayer for me. 

It's simple unlike most recent COD games with their gazillion different kill streak rewards and MLG quickscopers or Battlefield where it's just pure, utter chaos and a race to see who can get to da choppa first so they can then dominate the match - no fun for players who just want to be Infantry or even tanks from my experience (excluding BF2 - that was awesome). 

Homefront was pretty balanced and fun. You earn points from kills and stuff then use those points to spawn in a humvee, LAV, tank, scout heli or attack heli. There's different weapons and loadouts of course. You can control a drone to use against enemy players. Overall, simple, balanced and lots of fun. I never felt like any match was unfair or that any one was at a disadvantage - it always felt like you were playing on a nice, even playing field. Obviously skill and experience still helps but there's nothing crazy happening just because someone got a 20 kill streak and no one is invincible just because they earned enough to spawn in an attack heli. 

Unfortunately, the multiplayer is mostly dead but there is a small community that plays regularly and I have seen people on the servers at certain times of day - so not completely. It's just a shame that it's not alive enough that you can just hop in and out of a game whenever you please - if only there were bots...

[h1]Homefront[/h1]
[i]More like a "Slow Concussion" than a "No Russian"[/i]

[h1]Review[/h1]
Homefront. Homefront! HOMEFRONT! Where does one even begin? Throw out the tortured symbolism of America, the home of the free and brave, now shackled under the weight of a military occupation thanks to the Korean Army, and you are still left with a clunker of a game.

[b]Homefront[/b] is the NLOG of video games. Yes, we have all known one of them before, the I am "Not like other girls" girl, who think because they do things other women don't, that they're better than those other women. In [b]Homefront[/b]'s case, it's the marrying of guerrilla warfare to [b]Call of Duty[/b] bombast as the game tries desperately to get you to take it seriously as it constantly tries to one-up the juggernaut in this genre, the [b]Call of Duty[/b] franchise, while failing at almost every checkpoint. Featuring a serious and topical narrative that could be plucked right from the front pages of today's newspapers, if today's newspapers were reporting that North Korea had just invaded Georgia and not America.

Instead [b]Homefront[/b] overloads the game's narrative with a preposterous and unbelievable scenario that immediately removes the seriousness [b]Homefront[/b] was aiming to achieve in the storytelling department rendering it laughably bad. We can all agree that with [b]Call of Duty[/b], it's the kind of franchise in which you can check your brain at the door, but [b]Homefront[/b] promises so much more than it delivers. The joke is on Kaos Studios. [b]Spec-Ops: The Line[/b] this ain't. There is absolutely no food for thought here. In fact you can check [b]Homefront[/b] at the latrine. Just make sure you flush! 

Life under a dictatorship would probably be far better than having to deal with the Post-Traumatic Shock Syndrome that bedevils your caretaker, Connor Morgan, who will guide you though this ugly slice of unreality. No forget guide, he will scream and bark commands at you until he finally decides to martyr himself near the end of the game. If he hadn't chosen to go the martyr route, I would most certainly have silently and quietly snuck into his retirement condo and put a bullet between both his eyes. 

He is a complete skuzzy ignoramus who couldn't lead his way out of a paper bag even if he tried, let alone try to lead a revolution. Most of the game you will be instructed to "follow" him but you are better off just taking the lead. Every relationship presented in this game is simple as none of the characters ever emerge as more than paper thin caricatures. Most of the performances for each character is so overblown, you can almost see each character chew through the scenery rather than shoot through it.

I have no idea why anybody wanted to make this story into a game because its so unpleasantly overblown, and for the most part obnoxious, throwing reams and reams of enemies at you that never stop coming until you advance upwards through the level and reach a point where the game finally decides to stop marching them down the conga line so that the next conga line scenario can begin. If there's one thing I absolutely hate, that is a never ending spawn of enemies that just keep on coming at you until the game finally decides you have advanced through the level enough.

To paraphrase the late, the great Roger Ebert and put my own spin on his words, "I hated this game. Hated hated hated hated hated this game. Hated it. Hated every simpering stupid vacant and insulting moment of it. Hated the sensibility that thought anyone would like it. Hated the implied insult to the gamer by its belief that anyone would be entertained by it or let alone believe it".

[b]Homefront[/b] stands as one of the worst and most ingratiating games I have ever played. I don't hold out any hope that [b]Homefront: The Revolution[/b] will appeal to me at all after this fiasco. Now if only I could find someone who could erase this experience from my mind for good.

Run of the mill, generic COD clone from 2011. It's not a terrible game, but you can do so much better. From the chunky, corny, nationalist/xenophobic storyline straight out of any Red Dawn-obsessed fanboy's cringey wet dreams, to the mechanics, to the firearms selection, to the bad AI, this game plays like a bowl of lukewarm, plain oatmeal: sloppy and memorably bland.

I was excited to dive into "Homefront," a first-person shooter set in a future where the United States is occupied by a unified Korea. However, after spending some time with the game, I have to admit that my enthusiasm quickly diminished. While the concept and storyline had potential, the overall gameplay experience left me frustrated and unfulfilled.

One of the major issues I encountered with "Homefront" was the disappointing AI. In a game that heavily relies on teamwork and strategic gunfights, the lack of assistance from AI-controlled allies was incredibly frustrating. They often seemed clueless, failing to provide any meaningful support during battles. Rather than reacting tactically or engaging enemies effectively, they seemed content to stand idly by, making me feel like I was fighting alone against overwhelming odds. This lack of team coordination greatly detracted from the immersion and made me question the purpose of having AI allies in the first place.

Furthermore, the gameplay mechanics failed to evolve or innovate since its release. In 2023, when technology has advanced so much, "Homefront" feels dated and unremarkable. The controls were clunky at times, and the enemy AI lacked depth and creativity. It felt like I was participating in a generic shooting gallery rather than engaging in a compelling and immersive gaming experience.

While the initial concept of a United States under occupation seemed promising, the execution fell flat. The narrative was compelling but failed to capture the player's interest consistently, leaving me disconnected from the protagonist's struggle. The campaign felt short, lacking the depth and complexity that would have truly immersed me in the game world.

In conclusion, I must express my disappointment with "Homefront." The unhelpful AI, stagnant gameplay mechanics, and overall lack of innovation make it a poor choice for players seeking a captivating and engaging gaming experience. With so many other titles available in 2023 that push boundaries and offer more immersive gameplay, "Homefront" fails to deliver and is not worth investing your time in.

Homefront is the definition of a middle-of-the-pack 7/10 shooter—a game that hits every expected mark for a cinematic, narrative-driven FPS from the Xbox 360/PS3 era without ever quite breaking out of the mold.

 The Good

    A Solid, Grounded Premise: The game imagines a near-future occupied America under a unified Korean republic. The world-building in the opening act—seeing suburban neighborhoods turned into military zones—is genuinely compelling and sets a dark, tense tone.

    Competent Gunplay: The shooting mechanics are tight, punchy, and responsive. Weapon handling feels weighty, and the firefights deliver a satisfying impact, whether you're clearing suburban streets or defending key strongholds.

    Atmospheric Set Pieces: From fighting through an overgrown Golden Gate Bridge to tactical guerrilla strikes, the campaign packs in memorable moments that capture the feel of an underdog resistance force.

 The Flaws

    By-the-Numbers Design: Beyond its setup, the mission structure relies heavily on standard linear corridors, follow-the-NPC objectives, and scripted set pieces that felt familiar even in 2011.

    Brief Campaign: At around 4 to 5 hours, the single-player story ends right as the resistance narrative starts gaining real momentum, leaving several story threads feeling rushed.

    Inconsistent AI: Enemy and companion AI can be rigid, occasionally breaking the tension with predictable movement patterns or spotty cover mechanics.

 Verdict

Homefront doesn't redefine the cinematic first-person shooter, but it delivers a fun, nostalgic playthrough for fans of classic military FPS campaigns. It’s a solid, straightforward shooter that does its job well—a reliable artifact of its era.

A mediocre shooter that completely overshoots the characterization of both heroes and villains, making both a laughable caricature without displaying a shred of awareness of how tone-deaf its "we're dead-serious" attitude comes across.

Whatever intrigue the novel and close-to-home (literally) scenario evokes is thrown out of the window by hamfisted storytelling that paints the villains as absolute evil, while painting the heroes as virtuous paragons without any nuances or wink-wink awareness that the Wolfenstein games lend to their Nazi antagonists.

Take the United Korean Forces:
Mass Executions? Check.
Forced separations of parents/children? Check.
Mass-Graves? Check.
Over-the-top brutality? Check.
The list goes on and on through pretty much every horrible war crime in the book without consideration if it would make sense for an occupier to employ these tactics other than to come across as evil as possible.

The resistance?
Protecting mothers, babies? Check.
Cherishing community and self-sufficiency? Check.
Banding together to defeat the great evil? Check.
This difference is especially forced upon the player by moving the story from occupation territories, full of crying and screams of agony, to a resistance haven, filled with children's laughter and gentle music. Yes. it's that blatant and flat.
Koreans evil. Americans good.

Oh, and in true 2011-style, the main female sidekick,. Rianna, wears basically no armor, leaving room to show off her belly-button and cleavage. Because looking good is the prime objective in a warzone. While one may argue that the resistance may not have the same amount of equipment as the UKF, the complete lack of HELMETS and body armor creates a situation where the highly-armored Koreans made out of wet paper while skimpily-dressed Rinanna can take a rocket to the face.

Now, you might say that I shouldn't come here for the story - which is a silly angle as the scenario and context is the main draw - but the shooting also isn't here to save the day.

Ammo for weapons is strictly limited, forcing you to swap between them as you go. However, enemies carry a bazillion of different gun configurations, forcing to you hold a different gun every 30 seconds within a firefight. One may assume that a well-organized occupation force has a standardized loadout, when in fact the UKF seem to have a complete hodge-podge of armaments.

Speaking of armaments, for all the assumed technical and military superiority of the UKF, their tactics and technology all have laughable weaknesses. Take the ever-present sentry towers. To disable them requires nothing more than lobbing a grenade at the exposed fuel tank. A tank that is not only painted in bright white but also pointed out by red blinky lights. While most of that may be attributed to guiding the player, its heavy-handed hand-holding is never addressed by the characters or rationalized, making it stand out starker against the overly-serious backdrop of the story.

Overall, it might be interesting to briefly dabble in the game to explore the scenario and setting, but once that fluff has worn off there is nothing left but a very mediocre shooter with a story and characterization that may come straight out of a testosterone-fuelled fever dream of a 13-year-old.

Yet another game that I don't really hate that much but still, can't recommend to anyone for oh... so... many... reasons. There isn't much to say about this one. It's yet another one of those cheesy online-oriented [b]FPS[/b] with a few-hours-long story mode that exists just because and a pretty cheap aftertaste. We've seen many of those before and, well, here's (yet) another one of them. But you know what? That's not my problem with [b]Homefront[/b]. I mean, yes, there's no real [i]reason[/i] for it to exist. Without it being made? Nothing will change. Like... at all. This exact stuff (and way better) you can find in many other games of such kind. But at the same time... it's not so bad.

I grew up with [b]Tom Clancy[/b]'s novels, so naturally, I can totally dig all that cheesy-ass bull. I mean, the American forces fighting Korean invaders on [b]Golden Gate Bridge[/b]? I like that kind of stuff. Seriously, when you stop taking it seriously, it's just... I dunno, [i]fun[/i]. It isn't even about the countries or names. Heck, I didn't even have problems with [b]Mr. Clancy[/b]'s characters fighting my country in the novels. It's just that. A cheesy-ass entertainment and for what it is? It's [i]fun[/i]. Also, sure, [b]Homefront[/b] “story” takes only a few hours to beat, but let's just face it – the main dish here is multiplayer [i]and[/i] at least [b]Homefront[/b] has single player mode. That even tries to add a little ([i]ve-e-e-e-e-e-ery little[/i]) [b]ArmA[/b] aftertaste to the formula. Many other games, even those that were based on famous franchises like [b]Terminator[/b], did not. Like I said, I don't really mind this game. I mean... sure, we didn't ask for it. But why the heck not, right? So... why's the thumb down? [i]Well...[/i] where should I start?

First thing first – it's a dead game. That's it. Due to the [b]THQ[/b]s bankruptcy, all [b]Homefront[/b] servers were completely shutdown. With absolutely no hope for them to return. And, like I already said above, it's a multiplayer-oriented game with single player mode existing just to let publisher say that it is there. “[i]Hey! You don't like online shooters? We've got you covered since our game also has single player mode!!![/i]”. That's just how it works. Nobody cared about proper single player experience. Seriously, it's, like, five hours-long at best and most of the time there you'll either watch your characters walking and talking about some random crap, or die in agony during some heavily unpolished events (even though there are only seven short chapters here, the amount of “[i]Boom! You're dead![/i]” parts is just insane). Trust me, this game? It is not a single player experience you're looking for. And with multiplayer being dead... well... you've got the idea. Even with [b]90%[/b] off? It's just a waste of money.

Technically, I can stop here, but... well... there's more. Even if you're still considering five-hours-long cheesy [b]Tom Clancy[/b]-like story to be a good deal for, like, one or two bucks (don't even [i]think[/i] about paying the full price here!), there's still more crap to make you reconsider. For me, the biggest deal breaker was gamepad support. You may ask what kind of moron plays first-person shooters on personal computer with gamepad, but you know what? I like doing that. I mean, when it's about multiplayer, there's no other option but to use proper mouse and keyboard, but when it's about single player? I prefer my shooters on big [b]TV[/b] with gamepad, rather than on small monitor with mouse. Just because of that exact cinematic experience we all buy big [b]TV[/b]s for. And [b]Homefront[/b]? Even though it's a seventh generation title that was released for both [b]PlayStation 3[/b] and [b]Xbox 360[/b] (heck, it even got “platinum” re-releases on both systems), there's... no [b]XInput[/b] support here.

For those of us who don't know what that means, it means that your fancy-ass gamepads from [b]Microsoft[/b]'s systems ([b]Xbox 360[/b], [b]Xbox One[/b] and [b]Xbox Series X[/b], [i]man[/i], [b]Microsoft[/b] systems have terrible names...) won't work with this game properly. To play this game with gamepad on personal computer, you'll need one of those old [b]DirectInput[/b] gamepads like [b]Logitech Rumblepad 2[/b] or [b]Logitech F510[/b]. You know, the ones we used to play sixth generation titles like [b]Dreamfall: The Longest Journey[/b]. And even those won't work perfectly. For example, I was unable to make rumble feature work with those. Which is fun, since rumble worked perfectly fine with my [b]Xbox Series X[/b] gamepad (it was literally the only thing that worked properly there). Technically, you can make your gamepad work with this game through some third-party tools ([b]PC[/b] mustard race, [i]ho!~[/i]), but since setting this up would probably take longer than beating the story here... let's just say it doesn't worth it. In other words, gamepad support? It's screwed up here. Forget about it. You want to play this game? Play it with mouse. Even though (surprise-surprise), mouse support has its own issues (the one with the acceleration). Even something as simple as resolution selection comes with some problems that may lead you to manually editing [b]INI[/b] files or (again) using third-party tools ([b]PCGaming Wiki[/b] got you covered, not a sponsor).

In other words, it's a dead online-oriented game with a poor and cheesy four-hours long campaign that comes with a fair share of technical difficulties. A game that doesn't worth your time no matter how you look at it. Seriously, you don't need this game. Like... at all. Not for the full price (don't... even... think... about... it...) and not during the sale. You don't need [b]Homefront[/b] in your life. Like I said at the very beginning? It's one of those games that didn't have any reason to exist to begin with. And now? It's just dad. Dead and won't be missed. Dixi.

From what I've read, the general consensus on Homefront is that it's just average. After finally getting around to finishing it, I think the reviewers may have sold it a tad short. I mean, I wouldn't call it a masterpiece, but I also found very little wrong with it. I guess the biggest issue is that the single player (which is all I cared about) only took 4-5 hours to finish. So while it definitely wasn't worth the original asking price, now that it's only $20, it may not be a bad investment if you have ever had any interest in playing it. As far as the gameplay goes, it's pretty standard for a modern shooter. Mostly you shoot people (duh), but some levels mix it up with vehicle sections and other types of mechanics. The final level is also pretty epic. What sets Homefront apart from most shooters is the story, the premise being an alternate future where North Korea has occupied the US. All in all, it's a decent, but short game. Perfect for FPS fans to kill time on a rainy afternoon.
